```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import pathlib
import json
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import plotly.express as px
from scipy import stats

ROOT = pathlib.Path(".").resolve()
DATA = ROOT.parent / "data"

# --- Load CSA features ---
df = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "outputs" / "csa_features.csv")
df["csa2010"] = df["csa2010"].str.strip()

# --- Load BNIA actual eviction rate (2023, per 1k residents) ---
bnia = pd.read_csv(DATA / "bnia_evictions.csv")
bnia["csa2010"] = bnia["CSA2010"].str.strip()
df = df.merge(bnia[["csa2010", "evict23"]], on="csa2010", how="left")
df = df.rename(columns={"evict23": "bnia_eviction_rate"})

# --- Load GeoJSON ---
CSA_RENAME = {
    "Greater Lauraville":      "Lauraville",
    "Orchard Ridge/Armistead": "Claremont/Armistead",
    "Pigtown/Carroll Park":    "Washington Village/Pigtown",
    "Oliver/Johnston Square":  "Greenmount East",
    "Hampden/Remington":       "Medfield/Hampden/Woodberry/Remington",
    "Greektown/Bayview":       "Orangeville/East Highlandtown",
    "Hamilton Hills":          "Harford/Echodale",
}
gdf = gpd.read_file(DATA / "Community_Statistical_Areas.geojson")
gdf["csa2010"] = gdf["CSA2020"].map(lambda x: CSA_RENAME.get(x, x) if x else x)
gdf = gdf.merge(df, on="csa2010", how="left")

geo_dict = json.loads(gdf[["csa2010", "geometry"]].to_json())
for feature, row in zip(geo_dict["features"], gdf.itertuples()):
    feature["id"] = row.csa2010

# --- Pre-compute correlations ---
def pearson(x, y):
    sub = df[[x, y]].dropna()
    r, p = stats.pearsonr(sub[x], sub[y])
    return r, p, len(sub)

def bivariate_table(rate_col, exclude_extra=None):
    exclude = {
        rate_col, "csa2010", "eviction_count", "bnia_eviction_rate",
        "total_pop", "total_hh", "renter_hh",
        "total_residential_properties", "total_residential_units",
        "bnia_total_residential_props", "total_rental_units",
        "unique_owners", "units_top_10_owners",
        "eviction_rate_per_1k_residents", "eviction_rate_per_1k_households",
        "eviction_rate_per_1k_renter_hh", "eviction_rate_per_1k_rentals",
    }
    if exclude_extra:
        exclude |= set(exclude_extra)
    rows = []
    for feat in [c for c in df.columns if c not in exclude]:
        sub = df[[rate_col, feat]].dropna()
        if len(sub) < 10:
            continue
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(sub[rate_col], sub[feat])
        sr, sp = stats.spearmanr(sub[rate_col], sub[feat])
        rows.append({
            "feature": feat, "n": len(sub),
            "pearson_r": round(r, 3), "pearson_p": round(p, 4),
            "spearman_r": round(sr, 3), "spearman_p": round(sp, 4),
        })
    return (
        pd.DataFrame(rows)
        .assign(abs_r=lambda x: x["pearson_r"].abs())
        .sort_values("abs_r", ascending=False)
        .drop(columns="abs_r")
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )

r_w_concentration, p_w_concentration, _ = pearson("ownership_concentration_pct", "eviction_rate_per_1k_residents")
r_w_income,        p_w_income,        _ = pearson("median_hh_income",            "eviction_rate_per_1k_residents")
r_w_race,          p_w_race,          _ = pearson("pct_black_non_hisp",          "eviction_rate_per_1k_residents")
r_w_lowinc,        p_w_lowinc,        _ = pearson("pct_hh_income_under_25k",     "eviction_rate_per_1k_residents")
r_w_unemp,         p_w_unemp,         _ = pearson("unemployment_rate",           "eviction_rate_per_1k_residents")

r_b_concentration, p_b_concentration, _ = pearson("ownership_concentration_pct", "bnia_eviction_rate")
r_b_income,        p_b_income,        _ = pearson("median_hh_income",            "bnia_eviction_rate")
r_b_race,          p_b_race,          _ = pearson("pct_black_non_hisp",          "bnia_eviction_rate")
r_b_lowinc,        p_b_lowinc,        _ = pearson("pct_hh_income_under_25k",     "bnia_eviction_rate")
r_b_unemp,         p_b_unemp,         _ = pearson("unemployment_rate",           "bnia_eviction_rate")

r_cross, p_cross, n_cross = pearson("eviction_rate_per_1k_residents", "bnia_eviction_rate")

# --- Shared style ---
PLOTLY_TEMPLATE = "plotly_white"
MAPBOX_STYLE    = "carto-positron"
MAP_CENTER      = {"lat": 39.2904, "lon": -76.6122}
MAP_ZOOM        = 10
COLOR_SEQ       = px.colors.sequential.Reds
WARRANT_COLOR   = "#c0392b"
BNIA_COLOR      = "#2980b9"
```

## Two Ways to Measure Eviction

Eviction can be measured at two points in the legal process:

- **Eviction warrant filings** (this analysis, December 2024) — the moment a landlord initiates court proceedings. Many tenants self-evict after receiving a notice, leaving before their court date to avoid a formal record. The filing alone disrupts households, triggers informal credit damage, and burdens courts regardless of outcome.

- **Actual evictions** (BNIA Vital Signs, 2023) — cases that proceeded to a completed removal. This is the conventional measure, but it systematically undercounts displacement because self-eviction goes unrecorded.

Both rates below use the same denominator — **evictions or warrants per 1,000 residents** — for a direct comparison.

---

## Where Each Rate Is High

```{python}
#| label: map-warrants

fig = px.choropleth_mapbox(
    gdf, geojson=geo_dict, locations="csa2010",
    color="eviction_rate_per_1k_residents",
    color_continuous_scale=COLOR_SEQ,
    mapbox_style=MAPBOX_STYLE, center=MAP_CENTER, zoom=MAP_ZOOM,
    opacity=0.75, hover_name="csa2010",
    hover_data={"eviction_rate_per_1k_residents": ":.1f", "csa2010": False},
    labels={"eviction_rate_per_1k_residents": "Warrants per 1k residents"},
)
fig.update_layout(
    title="Eviction Warrant Rate — December 2024 (per 1,000 Residents)",
    margin=dict(t=50, b=0, l=0, r=0), height=500,
    coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="Warrants<br>per 1k res."),
)
fig.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: map-bnia

fig = px.choropleth_mapbox(
    gdf, geojson=geo_dict, locations="csa2010",
    color="bnia_eviction_rate",
    color_continuous_scale=COLOR_SEQ,
    mapbox_style=MAPBOX_STYLE, center=MAP_CENTER, zoom=MAP_ZOOM,
    opacity=0.75, hover_name="csa2010",
    hover_data={"bnia_eviction_rate": ":.1f", "csa2010": False},
    labels={"bnia_eviction_rate": "Evictions per 1k residents"},
)
fig.update_layout(
    title="Actual Eviction Rate — BNIA 2023 (per 1,000 Residents)",
    margin=dict(t=50, b=0, l=0, r=0), height=500,
    coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="Evictions<br>per 1k res."),
)
fig.show()
```

The two maps share broad geography — high-displacement neighborhoods in East and West Baltimore appear in both — but the warrant map shows higher rates in areas with concentrated landlord ownership that don't stand out as sharply in the BNIA map.

---

## How Well Do They Correlate?

```{python}
#| label: scatter-cross

fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="bnia_eviction_rate", y="eviction_rate_per_1k_residents",
    hover_name="csa2010", trendline="ols", template=PLOTLY_TEMPLATE,
    labels={
        "bnia_eviction_rate": "BNIA Actual Eviction Rate (per 1,000 Residents, 2023)",
        "eviction_rate_per_1k_residents": "Warrant Filing Rate (per 1,000 Residents, Dec 2024)",
    },
    title="Warrant filing rate vs. actual eviction rate — same denominator",
)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=8, opacity=0.7, color=BNIA_COLOR), selector=dict(mode="markers"))
fig.update_layout(height=460, margin=dict(t=60, b=40))
fig.show()
```

*Pearson r = `{python} f"{r_cross:.2f}"`, p = `{python} f"{p_cross:.4f}"` (n = `{python} n_cross` CSAs)*

A moderate positive correlation — the two measures broadly agree on which neighborhoods have elevated eviction pressure. But the relationship is far from 1:1, and the scatter below shows the divergence is structured, not random.

---

## What Predicts Each Rate?

The two measures are driven by almost entirely different structural factors.

### Ownership Concentration

## Full Bivariate Correlation Tables

### Warrant Filing Rate (per 1,000 Residents)

```{python}
#| label: bivariate-warrants

warrant_corr = bivariate_table("eviction_rate_per_1k_residents")
warrant_corr.style \
    .set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "thead th", "props": [("background-color", "#2c3e50"), ("color", "white"), ("font-weight", "bold")]},
        {"selector": "tbody tr:nth-child(even)", "props": [("background-color", "#f9f9f9")]},
        {"selector": "td, th", "props": [("padding", "6px 12px"), ("text-align", "left")]},
    ]) \
    .bar(subset=["pearson_r"], color=["#aed6f1", "#c0392b"], vmin=-1, vmax=1) \
    .format({"pearson_r": "{:.3f}", "pearson_p": "{:.4f}", "spearman_r": "{:.3f}", "spearman_p": "{:.4f}"})
```

## What the Divergence Means

The two measures agree on broad geography but diverge on causation:

- **Warrant filings** are primarily predicted by **ownership concentration** — concentrated landlords appear to use the court system as a portfolio management tool, filing across their holdings regardless of neighborhood demographics. Income, race, and unemployment are not statistically significant predictors.

- **Actual evictions** follow the standard Baltimore pattern: **income, race, and unemployment** are all highly significant (p < 0.001), while ownership concentration is not. Completed evictions trace structural vulnerability, not landlord filing behavior.

Both patterns matter. Tracking only completed evictions obscures the role that concentrated ownership plays in burdening the court system and pressuring tenants — many of whom self-evict before a judgment is ever entered.
